findings.source_passage: Ever and anon a bright, but, alas, deceptive idea would dart you through.—It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale.—It's the unnatural combat of the four primal elements.—It's a blasted heath.—It's a Hyperborean winter scene.—It's the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 2, the extended meditation on the painting
findings.why_it_matters: This rhetorically distinctive litany of guesses—with its dashes and escalating cosmic imagery—is among the most recognizable and critically discussed passages in the chapter; it establishes the painting as a figure for the novel's interpretive indeterminacy and is prosodically unique in Melville's repertoire.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full catalogue of guesses ('It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale … the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time') verbatim or near-verbatim; the dash-separated list is the signature shape and cannot be paraphrased away.

findings.source_passage: A boggy, soggy, squitchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man distracted.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 2, immediately after the description of the 'black mass'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is prosodically and lexically unique ('boggy, soggy, squitchy') and critically cited as exemplary of Melville's comic-sublime register; its erasure removes the tonal pivot that makes the painting passage work as both mock-sublime and genuinely portentous.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'A boggy, soggy, squitchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man distracted.'

findings.source_passage: like another cursed Jonah (by which name indeed they called him), bustles a little withered old man, who, for their money, dearly sells the sailors deliriums and death.
findings.why_it_matters: The draft retains 'deliriums and death' but omits '(by which name indeed they called him)'—the parenthetical is the interpretively loaded Jonah-naming, a motif that resonates throughout the novel, and the full sentence is critically cited for its biblical freight.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the parenthetical '(by which name indeed they called him)' to preserve the Jonah-naming motif.

findings.source_passage: Abominable are the tumblers into which he pours his poison. Though true cylinders without—within, the villanous green goggling glasses deceitfully tapered downwards to a cheating bottom. Parallel meridians rudely pecked into the glass, surround these footpads' goblets.
findings.source_locator: paragraph immediately following the bar description
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is a set-piece of Melville's satirical-moralistic voice—'footpads' goblets,' 'villanous green goggling glasses,' the fake measure marks—and is rhetorically and stylistically distinctive; its complete absence erases a voice-establishing digression critical to the chapter's tone.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the tumblers passage in full or near-full; the 'footpads' goblets' and 'cheating bottom' phrasing is the signature and must survive.

findings.source_passage: No man prefers to sleep two in a bed. In fact, you would a good deal rather not sleep with your own brother… sailors no more sleep two in a bed at sea, than bachelor Kings do ashore.
findings.source_locator: extended interior-monologue paragraph beginning 'No man prefers to sleep two in a bed'
findings.why_it_matters: This comic-philosophical digression on privacy in sleep is a sustained voice passage that establishes Ishmael's rationalising consciousness; its omission flattens the interior monologue that is central to the chapter's comic structure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least the opening proposition and the 'bachelor Kings' comparison to preserve the satirical register.

findings.source_locator: paragraph describing the Grampus crew, near end of that section
findings.why_it_matters: Bulkington's introduction—his brooding apart-ness, his physical description, and the repeated cry of his name—is an interpretively loaded passage (he is a figure critics return to repeatedly as an emblem of the novel's tragic dimension); the entire Bulkington episode is absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Bulkington passage: his physical description ('chest like a coffer-dam'), his slipping away unobserved, and the crew's repeated cry of his name.

findings.source_passage: the landlord procured the plane; and with his old silk handkerchief first dusting the bench, vigorously set to planing away at my bed, the while grinning like an ape. The shavings flew right and left; till at last the plane-iron came bump against an indestructible knot.
findings.source_locator: bench-planing episode, after Ishmael refuses to share the bed
findings.why_it_matters: The bench-planing scene is the chapter's central comic set-piece; its complete absence removes a sustained passage of physical comedy and voice-establishing absurdist detail that critics treat as emblematic of Melville's comic mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the planing scene, including 'grinning like an ape,' 'plane-iron came bump against an indestructible knot,' and Ishmael's reflection that no planing could 'make eider down of a pine plank.'

findings.source_passage: going up to him as cool as Mt. Hecla in a snow-storm—'landlord, stop whittling. You and I must understand one another… you persist in telling me the most mystifying and exasperating stories tending to beget in me an uncomfortable feeling towards the man whom you design for my bedfellow—a sort of connexion, landlord, which is an intimate and confidential one in the highest degree.'
findings.source_locator: Ishmael's long speech demanding an explanation about the harpooneer
findings.why_it_matters: This extended mock-legal oration ('you sir, you I mean, landlord, you, sir, by trying to induce me… would thereby render yourself liable to a criminal prosecution') is a signature voice passage—Ishmael's comic-pompous register at its most sustained and distinctive.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the speech in substantial form, particularly the 'Mt. Hecla' simile, the 'connexion, landlord' formulation, and the mock threat of criminal prosecution.

findings.source_passage: Ignorance is the parent of fear, and being completely nonplussed and confounded about the stranger, I confess I was now as much afraid of him as if it was the devil himself who had thus broken into my room at the dead of night.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Even as it was, I thought something of slipping out of the window'
findings.why_it_matters: The aphorism 'Ignorance is the parent of fear' is a recognisable Melvillean sententia that anchors the comic-philosophical register of the scene; its loss mildly flattens the narrator's self-aware moralising voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence verbatim or close to verbatim as part of Ishmael's internal reaction to Queequeg.

summary: The draft has multiple high-severity signature losses—the 'boggy, soggy, squitchy' / litany-of-guesses painting passage, the tumblers/footpads'-goblets digression, and the Bulkington introduction—plus several medium-severity voice flattenings (bench-planing scene, Ishmael's mock-legal oration, the privacy-in-sleep digression) that together constitute a substantial erasure of the chapter's distinctive voice and interpretive content.
